title: Effective agent design patterns in production — Laurie Voss, LlamaIndex

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is agent design patterns—chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator workers, and evaluator optimizers—and how to structure agent systems using LlamaIndex workflows. The patterns are presented as general-purpose agent architecture guidance, while LlamaIndex is explicitly a developer platform for building generative AI applications. The content is about designing and building agent systems, covering architecture patterns and implementation syntax. The talk assumes familiarity with RAG and agents but introduces design patterns and code syntax at an accessible intermediate level. This is a 15-minute conference talk recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript with supporting evidence anchors.

summary: Laurie Voss introduces LlamaIndex as a Python and TypeScript framework for building generative AI applications, particularly strong at building agents. Key products include LlamaParse (document parsing for PDFs, Word, PowerPoint), LlamaCloud (enterprise SaaS for document-to-retrieval-endpoint pipelines), and LlamaHub (open-source registry with 400+ models across 80+ LLM providers, pre-built agent tools, and integrations with vector databases and data sources). He defines an agent as semi-autonomous software that uses tools to achieve goals without explicit step-by-step instructions, noting that agents represent a dramatic departure from traditional programming because LLMs are given decision-making power. The best agent use cases involve turning large bodies of text into smaller ones — summarizing documents, interpreting contracts, processing invoices, applying regulations — rather than expanding small prompts into large outputs. He encourages thinking beyond chatbots toward integrating LLMs into existing software to handle unstructured inputs and produce structured data for regular systems. He explains RAG as essential for providing contextual data: embedding data into vectors, searching for relevant context, and feeding only the most relevant context to the LLM. He argues RAG will never die because sending less data is always cheaper, faster, and yields better answers. Critically, agents need RAG and RAG needs agents: layering an agent on top of RAG enables introspection, question decomposition, retry logic, and self-evaluation that naive top-k RAG cannot do. He then references Anthropic's December post codifying agent design patterns. Chaining passes LLM output to subsequent LLMs via LlamaIndex workflows with a built-in visualizer. Routing lets an LLM decide which tool or path to use via branches. Parallelization has two flavors: sectioning (same input processed differently, e.g., guardrails) and voting (same query sent to multiple tracks to reduce hallucination via majority or unanimous vote — if three different LLMs reach the same conclusion, it is probably not hallucination since LLMs hallucinate in different ways). Orchestrator workers use an LLM to decompose a complex multi-part question into several simpler questions answered in parallel and then aggregated into one coherent answer — this is how deep research works. Evaluator optimizers (also called self-reflection) use an LLM to evaluate whether the LLM has done a good job, generating feedback sent back to the original step in a loop; in LlamaIndex workflows this is implemented by creating a loop that sends control back to step one. The real power is combining all patterns to create arbitrarily complex workflows. He briefly shows LlamaIndex tool syntax: a Python function wrapped in a step wrapper, given to an agent which recognizes it as a tool. Multi-agent systems are created by feeding an array of function agents (each with a system prompt, LLM, and tools) into a multi-agent system that passes control between agents — technically one line of code. A tutorial notebook for building a deep research agent is referenced.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Agents are semi-autonomous software that use tools to achieve goals without explicit step specification — a dramatic departure from traditional programming where LLMs hold decision-making power
Good agent use cases involve reducing large text to smaller text (summarizing, contract interpretation, invoice processing), not expanding small prompts into large outputs
RAG will never die: sending less relevant context is always cheaper, faster, and produces better answers than feeding all data to the LLM every time
Agents and RAG are symbiotic — agents improve RAG accuracy via introspection, question decomposition, and self-evaluation; RAG provides agents with necessary contextual data
Voting parallelization reduces hallucination: if three different LLMs reach the same conclusion, it is probably not hallucination since LLMs hallucinate in different ways
Orchestrator workers pattern decomposes complex questions into simpler parallel sub-questions then aggregates answers — this is how deep research works
Evaluator optimizer (self-reflection) uses an LLM to evaluate its own output and loop back with feedback, implemented as a workflow loop in LlamaIndex
The real power of agent design patterns comes from combining all of them to create arbitrarily complex workflows
LlamaIndex multi-agent systems can be created in one line of code by feeding an array of function agents into a multi-agent system that passes control between agents
Thinking beyond chatbots toward integrating LLMs into existing software represents a much larger addressable market than chat interfaces alone

sections.title: Introduction and LlamaIndex Overview
sections.summary: Laurie Voss introduces himself as VP of Developer Relations at LlamaIndex and surveys the LlamaIndex ecosystem: a Python and TypeScript framework for generative AI, LlamaParse for document parsing, LlamaCloud for enterprise retrieval endpoints, and LlamaHub for integrations with 400+ models across 80+ LLM providers, pre-built agent tools, and adapters for data sources and vector databases.

sections.title: Agents: Definition and Use Cases
sections.summary: Defines agents as semi-autonomous software that uses tools to achieve goals without explicit step specification, representing a dramatic departure from traditional programming. Good use cases involve turning large text into smaller text (summarizing, contract interpretation, invoice processing). Encourages thinking beyond chatbots toward integrating LLMs into existing software to handle unstructured inputs and produce structured data.

sections.title: RAG: Why It Is Essential and Its Relationship with Agents
sections.summary: Explains RAG as essential for providing company-specific contextual data: embedding data into vectors, searching for relevant context, and feeding only relevant context to the LLM. Argues RAG will never die because sending less data is always cheaper, faster, and yields better answers. Critically, agents need RAG and RAG needs agents — layering an agent on top of RAG enables introspection, question decomposition, retry logic, and self-evaluation that naive top-k RAG cannot do.

sections.title: Agent Design Patterns: Chaining, Routing, Parallelization
sections.summary: References Anthropic's December post codifying agent design patterns. Covers chaining (passing LLM output to subsequent LLMs, implemented via LlamaIndex workflows with a built-in visualizer), routing (LLM decides which tool or path to use via branches), and parallelization with two flavors: sectioning (same input processed differently, e.g., guardrails) and voting (same query to multiple tracks to reduce hallucination via majority or unanimous vote). Orchestrator workers and evaluator optimizers are named but not yet covered.

sections.title: Orchestrator Workers, Evaluator Optimizers, and LlamaIndex Syntax
sections.summary: Completes coverage of Anthropic's five patterns. Orchestrator workers use an LLM to split a complex question into simpler parallel sub-questions then aggregate answers — how deep research works. Evaluator optimizers (self-reflection) use an LLM to evaluate its own output and loop back with feedback via a LlamaIndex workflow loop. The real power is combining all patterns. Briefly shows LlamaIndex tool syntax (Python function in a step wrapper) and multi-agent system creation (array of function agents fed into a multi-agent system, one line of code). References a tutorial notebook for building a deep research agent.
